en: No. 7439 Title: Khaḍgamālābhāṣya Author: Bhāskarācārya
Script: Devanāgarī;
Extent: 28 folios; Government Manuscripts Library, Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute, Pune (India).
I bow to the auspicious Śrī.
Even those such as Indra, Rudra, Brahmā, and Viṣṇu do not, by their giving, escape the power of death;
yet she who touches the feet of the virtuous wife is the witness against the Great Lord’s bestower of death, the God of Love.
"Come together and behold this most auspicious bride.
(1) The son of Gambhīrarāya, named Bhārati, who delights in the burden of the *Bhārata* and who holds the secret of the lotus feet of the divine teacher Śrī Rāma in his mind; (2)
He explains the extraction of the fifteen-fold garland-mantra arising from the fifteen syllables of the Vidyā, as found within the *Lalitāpariśiṣṭatantra*. (3) The Śrī Devī said:
"O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, omniscient one, treasury of compassion!
Please explain the mantra-garlands that arise from the Kādividyā.
Śrī Śiva said:
I shall proclaim the garland-mantras that bring great prosperity to the Great Queen;
by the mere recollection of which, all accomplishments (siddhis) are held in the palm of one's hand.
It is marked with one hundred and eighty-one names.

The Mālā-mantra of Tripurasundarī is encased by the word "namaḥ. (3) This [mantra] belongs to the lineage of the Guru; it possesses a radiant interior consisting of a golden garland of jewels numbering fifteen [tithis], fashioned by Śiva, and is priceless. It is the very key for unlocking the excellent jewel-casket that remains from Lalitā. (4)

(1a) First, there is the question of the Goddess directed toward Śiva: Although, according to the technical convention that "Vidyā-mantras are traditionally held to have female deities, while [other] mantras are held to have male deities," it would be logical for you alone to be the deity of the Vidyās dedicated to Tripurasundarī; nevertheless, because the word *mantra* possesses the power to denote both specific mantras and mantras in general—just as the term *manu* [denotes both specific Manus and the category of Manus in general]—there exist more than four hundred Kārṇa-mantras.
The expression is used because the designation "mālāmantra" indeed exists;
it serves to exclude [other mantras] such as the *prastāra-sahasrākṣarī*, the *upasthāna-sahasrākṣarī*, and so forth.
The meaning is: "speak of those fifteen in number which have arisen from the fifteen syllables of the Kāmarāja-vidyā. (1)
The Great Queen Lalitā is the great rising of the sun of gnosis; for those [who possess it], these are the *siddhis*.
The realized meaning is that they bestow the fruits of this world and the next, granting both enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*mokṣa*).
(2) Having specifically qualified [the deities] by their names, which are common nominal stems, there are two words, "namas," at the beginning and at the end of the collection of names.
He begins to enumerate those names, starting with "Tripurasundarī" and so forth.

(3) The six limbs, beginning with the heart and ending with the weapon; the six presiding deities of those [limbs], namely the six Nityās beginning with Kāmeśvarī and ending with Citrā; and the one Great Nityā—thus making sixteen.

The *deśikas* (guiding teachers) consist of the *guravas*, divided into the *divyaugha*, *siddhaugha*, and *mānavaugha*; these are respectively sixteen, eight, and four in number, totaling nineteen. The ten *siddhis*, beginning with *aṇimā*; the eight *mātṛs*, beginning with Brahmā; and including Tripurasundarī herself, there are sixty names. (4) The ten goddesses beginning with Sarvasaṃkṣobhaṇīmudrā;
the sixteen beginning with Kāmākarṣaṇī, whose names contain the term *ākarṣaṇī*; and those containing the term *anaṅga*, such as Anaṅgā. After that—
The six-limbed goddesses, the six *nityās*, and the sixteen *deśikās*;
the mothers of the *siddhis* numbering seventy-four (seven, four, and eight);
the *mudrā*, the *ākarṣaṇī*, the one called *anaṅgā*, and the sixteen *kuñjaras*. 4.
In sequence, Indra and the others, the ten directions, and all the deities of sound and so forth;
the deity of Speech (Vāk), Heti, and the great eight groups of eight deities;
then, O Great Bhaṭṭārikā, the single portion of the Great Bhaṭṭārikā.

*Kusumādyaḥ* means eight, numbering the same as elephants (*kuñjara*). The word *kramāt* (in order) applies to both [sides] by way of the "lamp on the threshold" (*dehalī-dīpaka*) maxim. *Indrāḥ* are fourteen. *Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇyādyāḥ* [are fourteen]. *Sarvasiddhimadādyāḥ* are ten. *Sarvajñādyāḥ* are also ten, numbering the same as the directions (*dik*). These three groups consist of words containing the term *sarva*. Together with the groups beginning with the *mudrās*, these six groups of deities reside in their respective distinct wheels (*cakra*), with two names at the end of each wheel.

(2a) This will be explained later. Thus, there are eighty [names]. Taken together, there are one hundred and forty names. 5. The eight goddesses of speech, beginning with Vaśinī, constitute the seventh wheel. When combined with the *hetis*—the deities of the weapons—they become "great" (*mahatyaḥ*), meaning they possess the word *mahā*. Since it is stated that they are divided into four groups of four according to the principle that "eight should be equal," [they are so designated].

(The second) is the fourth group; the eighth wheel is [the same]. "Mahābhaṭṭārikā" is the vocative address to the Goddess; "Mahābhaṭṭārikā" is the second [instance], which has already been stated as a constituent part of the mantra. "Ekalā" means the deity is indeed one. The ninth wheel: at the end of each pair of wheels, there are two names each, totaling twenty-three. Altogether, this makes one hundred and sixty-three. At the end of each of those: at the conclusion of each individual group among the aforementioned groups of deities of the nine wheels, there is one name for each of the nine wheels beginning with Trailokyamohana, formed from a single line [of the text].

Following that, one name each from the group of nine beginning with Makaṭā and the others should be assigned as two names [each]. The total count, however, remains the same. The meaning of "atha" (then) is that it refers to the pair of names of the Cakrayoginīs recited after the Mahābhaṭṭārikā. (7) The nine names beginning with Tripurā belong to the Cakreśvarīs; thereafter, there are likewise nine further names.
The epithets of the Sovereign of the Ninth Wheel (*navamacakreśvarī*) are composed of the word *mahāmahā*. Then, all the subsequent names are combined to show one hundred and eighty-one names.

It has already been stated that the word *namaḥ* should be placed at the beginning and the end of this collection. Therefore, after the final *namaḥ*, the two syllables *te triḥ* constitute the essential form (*svarūpa*).
This means: *śucipriyā vahnijāyai svāhā*. (8)
At the end of each of those wheels and for the yoginīs, there are nine names;
then there are nine names for the Cakreśvarīs, and after that, nine great and most magnificent names; then [comes] "Triḥśucipriyā."

O Great Goddess, this Mālā-mantra, beginning with the three Tāras, bestows all fruits; it is obtained through the lineage of transmission (saṃpradāya) and is difficult to attain even for Brahmā, Indra, and the other gods. (8–9)

The *tāra*—the syllable *oṃ*—should be placed before the initial word *namaḥ*. This entire composition, beginning with the *praṇava* (*oṃ*) and ending with *svāhā*, should be encapsulated by three *tāras*.

He states this very point as "ramaya": first, the composition should be encapsulated by the *ramā-bīja* at the beginning and the end, accompanied by the *śrī-bīja*; furthermore, it [should be] characterized by the *māyā-bīja*.

The composition, distinguished by both [the *aiṃ* and *hrīṃ* mantras], should be enclosed (*saṃpuṭita*) with the *aiṃ* mantra at the beginning and end; this is to be done together with the *vāk* (Aiṃ), *māyā* (Hrīṃ), and *kamalā* (Śrīṃ) mantras, which are well-known as the "Triple Tārā" (*tritārī*) in the *Kalpasūtra*. With the intention that there are two instances of the word *namaḥ*, three instances of the word *svāhā*, and the seed-syllables of truth (*satyabīja*) are also words, the excess of ninety-three is stated. [This results in] one hundred and eighty-one.

Enveloped again and again by delightful illusion and speech, there are thus one hundred and ninety-three words in the garland. (10) Even though only the nominal stems (*prātipadika*) have been extracted here, they are called "words" (*padāni*) with the intention of including the case-endings that will be described later. (10)

Mantras are of three types based on the distinction between those having Śakti as the deity, those having Śiva as the deity, and those having both as the deity. Regarding the nominal bases (prātipadika) mentioned, in the case where Śakti is the deity, they should be formed with the feminine suffixes *ṅī* and *p* according to the grammatical rules (*lakṣaṇa*). In the case where Śiva is the deity, they remain as they are. In the case where both are the deities, the meaning is that each pair of words should be recited in the form of a conjunction (*samuccaya*). Because the compound "stripuṃmithuna" is a word consisting of a verse-line (*padyātman*), there is no occasion for the application of the compound-final suffix (*samāsāntapratyaya*) such as in "strīpuṃsa. This is stated with the intention of indicating the specific nature of the *mālā-mantra*.

Thus ends the indication of the feminine gender. Those *mālā-mantras* are each fivefold: three are pure (*śuddha*), being devoid of prefixes; three have "namas" at the end, being joined with the word "namaḥ" at the end of each name; and [the remaining] three have "svāhā" at the end, with "svāhā" following each nominal stem (*prātipadika*).

The three *pallavas* are *tṛptiḥ*, *tarpa-yāmi*, and the word *na tu tṛpyatu*. The three final names, followed by the two words *jayaḥ* and *jaya-jaya*, constitute the *mālā-mantra* for each [name], O Goddess; it is threefold according to the distinction of female, male, and couple. These are fivefold when ending with *śuddha-namaḥ*, *svāhā*, *tṛptiḥ*, and *jayaḥ*. (11)
The Śakti-mālā is fivefold, and the Śiva-mālā is likewise;
the Dvaṃdva-mālā is also similar. Thus, there are fifteen [mālās] in sequence.
They are pure [mantras], ending with *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, *tarpaṇa*, and *jaya*.

In all garlands whatsoever, there shall be fivefold functions. The pure [function] consists of mere perfect awakening; by that, the recitation is prescribed. Worship should be performed mentally, and one should say, "I worship the Pādukā. 13–14.
The utterance "svāhā" is used in the *homa* (fire sacrifice), and "tarpayāmi" (I satisfy) in the *tarpaṇa* (libation).
The fifth [type of application] is said to be praise (*stuti*), arising from the combination of two *jaya*s.
Thus, the fivefold application occurs in the three types of garlands (*mālā*). Therefore, fifteen [applications] are declared for the garlands and their offshoots (*apallava*).
(4a) The meaning is that for those [mantras] there are these three, such that there are fifteen garland-mantras (*mālāmantra*).
He explains this very point with two [verses]: "The applications of the garland-mantras are twofold. (12, 13)
Now, he establishes their application according to the characteristics of the pure (*śuddha*) and other categories by means of three [verses]:

"Here, the words 'worship' (*pūjana*), 'oblation' (*homa*), and 'libation' (*tarpaṇa*) [are used] for the *Śrī Lalitā Mantra* which bestows its fruits and victory (*jaya*). And for the pure mantras ending with 'victory', the vocative case is used among the pronouns. (16)
The traditional usage is that [the mantras] end in *svāhā* or end in *namaḥ*.
O fair-complexioned one, this is the distinction among the five types of garlands; for the second [garland], those ending in *tarpayāmaḥ* are employed. (17–18)

Because it will be stated later that worship is accomplished by the power of the mantra alone even in the absence of flowers, clarified butter, and water; and because the seven-syllable formula "I worship the *pādukā*" (*namoṃtāsu pādukāṃ pūjayāmi*) should also be joined with the word "namas," as indicated by the particle "ca" (and), and that [word] should be placed immediately after "namaḥ" according to the order of recitation. Regarding the three types of garlands, since each is fivefold, the meaning is that there are fifteen [varieties]. 14, 15, 16.
The vocative case is the first person singular of the perfective participle (*saṃbuddhi*). The dative case is the traditional one;
for it is prescribed by such rules as "namas, svasti, svāhā," etc., when used in conjunction with those [words]. This is because the verb *tarpayati* (to satisfy) requires an object.
Only the second case-ending (accusative) is correct. The plural forms such as "śuddhānām" and so forth refer to each of those three mantras.

From the five syllables of the Kāmarāja-vidyā beginning with *ka* and ending with *hṛllekhā* (*ha*), five Śakti-mālā mantras are produced in sequence; from the six syllables beginning with *ha* and ending with *la*, the Śaiva mantras are formed; and from the six syllables beginning with *māyā* and ending with *māyā*, the Mithuna mantras are formed.

From the power (śakti) and from Śiva—the couple—there arise, in sequence, three groups of five. From each individual letter beginning with 'ka', the Kādividyā emerges. Therefore, in all the Āgamas, these fifteen-fold garlands are secret.

Adorned with the heart-mantras *tritārī*, *tāra*, and *hṛdaya*, together with eighty-one invocations ending in the vocative case, and further embellished by the word *namaste* followed by the three fires (*trivahni*) and their consorts (*dāra*),
this is the pure primordial nature (*prakṛti*) whose presiding deity is Śakti, [the essence] of the armies, the juices, and the garlands. (20–21)
[They are] addressed to the deity.

(19) For this reason—namely, because they are produced from fifteen syllables—those garlands, which are *mālā-mantras*, are [prefixed] with the *tritārī* (the three *tāras*), namely *oṃ*, *hrīṃ*, and *śrīṃ*.

*Tāra* is the *praṇava* (*oṃ*); *hṛdaya* is the word *namaḥ*. There are one hundred and eighty-one names, beginning with "Tripurasundarī" and so forth; these are the imperial names (*saṃmrājñāni*). (20)

“Sambuddhiḥ” means the vocative case in the singular; “tadantāḥ” refers to those [mantras] ending in that [vocative]. “Namaste trir iti svarūpām” refers to the form [of the mantra] as "namaste" repeated three times. “Vahnidārāsvāhāśabdaḥ” means those joined with the words *vahni*, *dārā*, or *svāhā*. Since these [mantras] are dedicated to Śiva as their deity (*śivadevatya*) and also to the dual deities (*dvaṃdvadevatya*), he says [the following] to distinguish between those two: “śaktīni. This refers to the remaining garland-mantras (*srajāṃ avaśiṣṭamālāmantrāṇām*) of the others. 21.

"The other fourteen are its modifications"—this is precisely the meaning he concludes. [He says: "Ending with *namaḥ*": although only the nominal stems were previously extracted, [the forms] ending in *namaḥ*, those beginning with the *śakti*-mantras, those ending in *jaya*, and those ending in the *mithuna*—these fourteen should be known as the modifications (*vikṛti*) of this [mūla-mantra], namely the *mālā*-mantras. (22)

O lady of excellent hips, even with five mouths, it is not possible to describe the greatness of the seven- and eight-fold garlands, even in hundreds of years. For one devoid of general devotion, even the fifteen [syllables] of the garland-mantra are merely corruptions; nevertheless, since there is no evidence for such being a mantra at the time of extracting the syllables, [they are not so].

Since [the mantra] will be extracted with the vocative case ending itself—as in the passage beginning "The extraction of the name Saṃbudhyaṃtā, the awakening of the accomplishment of Tripurā"—it is precisely such a Śaktimālā and so forth that constitutes the *prakṛti* (base form). In the phrase "satyāṣṭasrajam," the singular number is an archaic usage (*ārṣa*). [The mantras are] for those who are *sādhya*: those who are incurable by the medical treatments of the science of medicine, those who are merely palliable (*yāpya*), and those who are difficult to cure, yet still curable.
By means of easily remediable ailments and diseases; 23, 24, 25, 26.
By means of worship and specific dwellings;
27. The three words beginning with "flowers" (*puṣpa*) are indicative of all materials required for that [worship]. By these mantras, flowers, and so forth, [the performance of] worship and the like—
One should recite ten or five garlands daily once;
thus liberated from great sins, one shall obtain all merit.
Having repeated seven or eight garlands for a period of seven or eight days, [one attains the same].
"Draw near the enchanting bride who is to be won;
having performed this for one month with an excellent garland of seven or eight [strings], one is freed from the three kinds of diseases known as curable, manageable, and incurable. (25–26)
One who constantly recites the mantra seven or eight times a day becomes a personification of merit;
like a blazing fire, he is beheld there by spirits and *pūtanas*.
Through the power of the mantra’s efficacy, [he performs] worship, fire-offerings, or libations.
Even in the absence of flowers, clarified butter, and water, success is achieved through recitation alone.

One should not fall into the error of thinking that this instruction on substitutes is intended for something that can actually be performed [as a primary act], because these items have no application in rituals such as worship. Nor is it the case that...

Because the application (*viniyoga*) of a mantra whose indicative mark (*liṅga*) requires another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) to establish its general connection with that [rite] belongs only to such a [mantra].

And therefore, the triad of mantras ending in *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, and *tarpaṇa* is applied even to the fruits arising from worship (*pūjā*), fire-oblation (*homa*), and libation (*tarpaṇa*). As for the phrase "even in the absence of flowers," this is merely a praise intended to suggest the superiority of the present recitation (*japa*) in comparison to the respective worship and other rites to be accomplished. [This applies] to the pure [mantra] ending in *jaya*.

One who is unable to perform the recitation of seven or eight garlands every day should instead recite [the mantra] dedicated to Prakṛti, known as Śuddhaśakti, at the three junctions of the day; that person enjoys the same fruit that arises from the recitation of all the garlands. (29)

The seer (*ṛṣi*), meter (*chandas*), deity (*devatā*), and application (*viniyoga*) are each distinct. (30) The application for *japa* and praise has already been stated previously. As for the pure rosary (*śuddhamālā*), its status as a substitute during times of distress for daily worship will be explained later. (28) This is a substitute for the collective *japa* of all fifteen rosaries, but not for each one individually. However, the number of days prescribed for that optional rite must certainly be observed. (29)

All [rites] such as attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*) arise from the recitation of the entire *mālā-mantra* or from the collective recitation (*samaṣṭi-japa*). The Seer (*ṛṣi*) is the one who perceived the mantra. The Metre (*chandas*) is that which delimits the number of syllables in the mantra. The Deity (*devatā*) is that which is propounded by the mantra. The Application (*viniyoga*) is the relationship between the subordinate and the principal (*aṅgāṅgībhāva*). (30) — — — — — — (6b)

The fifteen [elements] to be described later will also be stated as distinct qualifiers for those two [groups], each being unique. (31) The word *yat* functions as a particle (*pādapūraṇa*). According to Amara, "pada," *aṅghri*, and *caraṇa* are masculine or neuter. The term *dṛśaḥ* is in the genitive singular; it is treated as a singular compound because it denotes a part of a living being (*prāṇyaṅga*).
The principles (*tattvas*) consist of the five organs of action, the five organs of cognition, and the principles of ego (*ahaṃkāra*), intellect (*buddhi*), and mind (*citta*). (32)
And regarding the principles of *pradhāna* and *puruṣa*, one should first mention the presiding deities beginning with Varuṇa and so forth, and then recite the verse concerning the fruit;
furthermore, the wise person should state the attributes of both the seer (*ṛṣi*) and the deity. (31)
I am the presiding deity of the anus, the generative organ, the hands, the nose, the tongue, and sight; likewise of the skin, the ear, the sense organs, the intellect, and the mind.
Varuṇa and the others are the presiding deities of the primary elements and the principle of the individual soul (puruṣa).
The twelve Ādityas, ending with Viṣṇu, are those who appear at dawn, midday, and sunset.
[There are] fifteen Ādityas. The sages of the fifteen garlands are, in order: obeisance to the sage Varuṇa-Āditya, the presiding deity of the organ of generation.

The application [of the mantras] is in the two pentads beginning with "ityādi. In the final pentad, [the sequence begins] with "ahaṃkāratattvādhiṣṭhāyine aṣṭādityāya" and so forth. In the final triad, [it begins] with "brahmātmane prātarādityāya" and so forth. (33) He designates Varuṇa and the others, twelve in number, by means of the passage beginning with "varuṇa. (34–35)
The word *jagat* is a synonym for the world (*jagatī*).
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva are the souls; these are the fifteen ṛṣis.
Varuṇa, Mitra, Dhātṛ, Aryaman, Aṃśumat, and Bhaga—34.
Indra, Vivasvat, Pūṣan, Savitṛ, Tvaṣṭṛ, and Viṣṇu;
now the meters of the fifteen-fold garlands are described in order:
Gāyatrī, Uṣṇih, Anuṣṭubh, Bṛhatī, and Paṅkti.
Triṣṭubh, Jagatī, Patijagatī, Śaṅkarī, and Atiśaṅkarī;
Aṣṭi, Atyaṣṭi, Dhṛti, Atidhṛti, Pañcadaśī, and Kṛti—now their deities are described; listen attentively, O beloved. (36–37)

If [it is argued that] in the Śruti passage "if one takes up the world as the *samāgrāyaṇa* cup," there is seen an interpretation stating that it is a *sāman* produced upon a verse (*ṛc*) in the *jagatī* meter; [in response:

the two words ending in long vowels (*aṣṭā-aṣṭī*) may either be a compound of two words ending in short vowels, or [the gender] is feminine with reference to the specific object qualified by the term "fifteen-fold meter" (*pañcadaśachandaḥkṛti*).

Now, in the first *mālā-mantra*, there are forty-three *gāyatrī* meters; among these, the last one is *nicṛt*. In this manner, its form as a fist (*muṣṭi*) and so forth should be inferred. In reality, although there is a great deal of variation—both deficiency and excess—in the number of syllables for each respective meter, the knowledge of that specific meter by means of that very [number] is solely for the sake of the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭārtha*). This has been analyzed by us in the *Chando-bhāskara* and other works. (36–37)

The three lords of the worlds— Amaruta and Marutvat— and the letters of the beginning, middle, and end, correspond respectively to the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas. Furthermore, the two letters of Vyoman and Candramas bestow enjoyment and liberation, respectively.
Likewise, the eleventh and fourth [syllables] would also be thus, provided they possess their respective qualifiers:

*hrīṃ* for Bhuvananāthā, *marut* (the letter *ka*) for *hrīṃ*, and *marutvat* (the letter *la*) for *kakāra*. Regarding the phrase "beginning and end": in the *Kādividya*, there are indeed three instances of *hrīṃ*. Among them, that situated in the first *kūṭa* is *sāttvika*; that in the final *kūṭa* is *rājasa*; and that in the middle *kūṭa* is *tāmasa*. The same applies to the three instances of *ka* and the three instances of *la*.

The three qualifiers—sāttvika and so forth—should be inferred for the three *hrīṃ* syllables. This means that those situated in the first, third, and middle *kūṭas* are sāttvika, rājasa, and tāmasa, respectively.

(38) [Regarding] the *hakāra* of the sky (*vyoman*) and the *sakāra* of the moon (*candramas*): in the second *kūṭa*, the first *haṃkāra* bestows enjoyment (*bhoga*), and the second bestows liberation (*mokṣa*). Likewise, the second *sakāra* bestows enjoyment.

The third [vowel] is the bestower of liberation. The eleventh vowel is *ekāra*. The fourth is *īkāra*; both of these, respectively, bestow enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*mokṣa*). In the reading "turīyā api," the word division is indeed at the dual ending. Regarding the substitute vowel *va* (in *vakāra*), there are the seats of the venerable Varṇabhaṭṭārikā, wherein the two Śivas reside in various places.
The two deities, distinguished by their respective names, are Kāmeśvara and Śiva.
Lalitā alone is declared to be the substantive (viśeṣyā) in relation to Śiva as Mahābhaṭṭārikā.
The Śakti who dwells upon the lap of Śiva is the primary one among the five Śaktis.

Because the elision is prescribed by way of an optional alternative (*vikalpa*). The phrase "in this manner" (*evam*) and so forth connects with what follows. (39) The fifteen phonemes (*varṇa*) themselves are the venerable lords (*bhaṭṭāraka*). The meaning is that, in the manner previously described, they are to be formed together with their respective qualifiers. And those phonemes are the seats (*pīṭha*), because Śiva and Śakti are established therein. Regarding all those hundred and eight seats of the Goddesses and sixty-eight seats of Śiva which are described in the *Purāṇas*, such as the *Padma-purāṇa* and the *Skanda-purāṇa*:

(8b) The names of Śiva and the names of Śakti are well known to be entirely distinct. In this context as well, they are likewise distinct; these names will be explained later in detail. Among them, for the names of Śiva, "Kāmeśvara" alone is the substantive term (*viśeṣyapada*). Where the name is simply "Kāma," as in the *Prakṛtimālā*, there [it is used].

Because of the application or non-application of the word *kāmeśvara* twice, the word *śiva* is stated for the sake of clarification that it must be employed together with the word *śiva*. Furthermore, it should be understood according to the tradition that this word occupies the position of the substantive (*viśeṣya*) alone.
As for the names of the Śaktis, however, the substantive word is simply *lalitā*.
Śiva, the Great Lord (Mahābhaṭṭāraka), has Lalitā as his ornamented lap.
In the Śaiva group of five deities, there is a pair consisting of two in union:
Kāmeśvarī with Kāmeśvara, and Ekālā with Ekavīra. 42.

The Goddess Īśvarī is cherished by the Lord Īśvara and by Lalita. (43) That [mantra] is headed by the title *Mahābhaṭṭārikā*. Thus, for the fivefold mantra of Śakti, the application is as follows: "Obeisance to the deity Amuka-Lalitā-Mahābhaṭṭārikā, who resides upon the lap of Amuka-Kāmeśvara and is established in the Sāttvika-Kakāra-Bhaṭṭāraka-pīṭha," and so forth. Because of the predominance of Śakti, he calls this the "Fivefold Garland of Śiva" (*śivamālāpañcaka*). (41)

(9a) Regarding "Lalita": the meaning is that the ritual application (*prayoga*) is performed according to the formula, "Salutation to the deity Kāyā, who is adorned by Mukalalitā and resides at the seat of the Great Lord (*mahābhaṭṭāraka*) Kāmeśvara," and so forth. He speaks of the fivefold garland of couples (*dvaṃdvamālāpañcaka*) with the words "of the couple" (*dvaṃdvasya*). The couple (*mithuna*) of the two, Śakti and Śiva, is the primary [element].

Therefore, it is established that in both cases, because the term *mahābhaṭṭāraka* serves as the headword, the word *mithuna* (couple) must be employed at the end of the *dvandva* compound. The practical application should be inferred in such a manner as: *namaḥ amuka-lalitā-bhaṭṭārikā-amuka-kāmeśvara-mahābhaṭṭāraka-mithuna-devatāyai* (Salutation to the couple-deity consisting of the venerable lady Amuka-Lalitā and the great venerable lord Amuka-Kāmeśvara), and so forth. Now, he sequentially indicates the names to be inserted in place of "Amuka. Here, in the first pentad, masculine endings are used. The third case ending is used in the sense of accompaniment (*sahārthe*).

The primacy of Śiva’s name [is established] because the powers alone are designated by the nominative case; however, their primacy is [relative], while their association consists in the state of having Śiva as their abode. But in the second pentad, due to the reversal of the case endings of the words "Śiva" and "Śakti," the relationship of subordinate and principal is also reversed; their association, however, consists in the state of being adorned by the circle of powers.

In the third group of five, however, because of the dual designation of "woman and man" (*strīpuṃsayaḥ*), it is implied that the meaning of both words is primary. Regarding the eighth mantra, the form *kamala* (without the feminine suffix) is used instead of *kamaleti* (with the feminine suffix *ī*) for the sake of conforming to the meter. The term *manoriti* refers to the *tarpaṇīyamālā-mantra*. *Hiraṇyabāhuḥ* is simply *hiraṇyabāhuḥ* [the compound being analyzed as such]. The mention of *hiraṇyapūrva-kaśipuṃ* is for the purpose of following the established tradition; the rest is clear. (43–47)
With Hṛllekhā he is considered Halika;
with Sarasvatī, Sarvajña; with Kamalā, Kālamardana (44);
and joined with Haravallabhā, Maheśvara becomes Haranātha.
Lakṣmyāyukta, Lalajjihva, Hiraṇya, Hṛdayendra, and Hara;
then the two Bhaṭṭārakas, namely Sakalajananī and Sakaleśvara;
and thereafter, in Śiva, those named Kāmakoṭi and Karuṇākara. (45–46)
The deities are the playful beauty and the hero of the fourteenth Manu, as well as Hari, the Lord, Hiraṇya, and the others, who are the arms.
O beloved, listen attentively as I declare their application (viniyoga). 47.
The sword, the power of sandals, collyrium, the accomplishment of the subterranean cave,
the accomplishments of speech, body, and iron, eternal bliss, and liberation— these fifteen are proclaimed, along with the eight siddhis beginning with atomization (aṇimā).
(10a) Subsequently, subjugation, attraction, delusion, and immobilization— these fifteen [mantras] all lead to the fruit of eternal bliss. 50.
He obtains such a sword that, with it held in his hand,
he will indeed become the sovereign emperor who enjoys the rule over the eighteen great continents.
Your devotee obtains such a pair of sandals.
When, by the mere act of stepping, he traverses the three worlds in an instant;
having obtained the perfected ointment and with eyes anointed by it, every devotee of yours, becoming prosperous, beholds the treasure. (52–53)

Having blocked the entrance to the netherworld (Pātāla), your devotee who has attained siddhi from those practitioners of yoga residing in the depths of Pātāla shall become happy. (54) *Viniyoga* means the relationship between the primary and subordinate parts (*aṅga-aṅgī-bhāva*), that is to say, the capacity to produce a result. This will become clear through the verses to be spoken later concerning the nature of the *siddhis*, such as the sword (*khaḍga*) and so forth.

The three distinct fruits are: mastery over speech, mastery over the body, and mastery over metals (*lohasiddhi*). Although one should say "the accomplishments" (*siddhayaḥ*), the use of the form "sidhya" is for the sake of metrical conformity.
Mastery over the eight powers, beginning with *aṇimā*, constitutes a single fruit. (Verses 48, 49, 50).
Now, he states the verses that must necessarily be recited at the commencement of the recitation (*japa*).
(10b) "Such a sword," and so forth. Having struck even those standing at a distance with that which is held in the hand, it returns to the hand again and again. [Verses 51–54].
Due to the distinctions of silver, copper, brass, bell-metal, lead, tin, bronze, and iron, there are eight types of metal. [Verses 57–65].

For those mantras for which the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) has not been explicitly stated, one should perform two sets of the six-limbed placement using the six long vowels along with *hṛllekhā* (the seed-syllable *hrīṃ*). After performing the two sets of six-limbed placement following the [assignment of] seers (*ṛṣi*) and so forth, and having meditated [on the deity], one should mentally [apply them] at the commencement of each respective mantra.
Speech-perfection (*vāksiddhi*) is said to be twofold, effecting both cursing (*śāpa*) and grace (*anugraha*).
And your devotion takes the form of great poetic genius; that is its abode.
By means of it, O devotee, your body—which is as fair as molten gold—is never subject to decay anywhere at any time. 55–56.
O Śivā, by the touch of the hand of your devotee, even the eight kinds of iron attain the state of gold,
just as one attains equality with Śiva.
Those qualities such as minuteness and magnitude, which are fashioned by mere will, [are likewise attained].
These natural qualities shall belong to the bodies of your devotees.
(58) By offering their own bodies, wealth, and lives like one's own servants, kings and others who have been brought under control serve your devotee. (59)
(11a) Even those women who are enclosed within iron walls and bound with fetters come forth indeed when they are drawn by your devotees. 60.
O Ambikā, by the mere glance of you,
men, women, kings, and others who are confused regarding what ought and ought not to be done become [awakened].
O Goddess, having beheld your devotee, [you grant the purification] of body, senses, and mind.
By subduing his enemies through immobilization, he turns them away from their respective tasks.
Dharma, Artha, Kāma, and Mokṣa—this fourfold aim—he, your devotee, bestows upon his own devotees without effort. (62–63)

O Supreme Goddess, for those men who worship Your feet, these two types of bliss— the supramundane and the mundane— are always easily attained. That Goddess who bestows worldly enjoyment does not grant liberation while living.
Lalitā, however, bestows both liberation and enjoyment.
(65) The meaning is that one should recite these fifteen verses after the ritual application (viniyoga). (66)
One should recite it.

Then, O Goddess, one should mutter the *mālā-mantras* according to each specific desire. (66) Thus ends [this section] from the work composed by the son of the venerable Dhārā-upapada-Gambhīrādhvarika, which is rendered meaningful here through the names of the Guru’s arts.
(11b) In the procedure for extracting [the mantras] from the garland, the jewel-casket, and the peg, the first chapter, concerning the extraction, is completed.

Chapter Two. Now, at the beginning of the second chapter, the Goddess asks again—clearly. Then he begins the extraction of the mantras by means of the half-verse. The three *tārīs* are explained as being the *praṇava*.

*Tripurasundarī* ends with a short vowel (*-ī*). Regarding the six-limbed deities (*ṣaḍaṅgadevatā*) who are to be worshipped within her body, he speaks in one verse and a quarter: from *hṛdayāt*. From the word *hṛdaya*, the word *devi* follows; at the end of that is the phrase *śiro devī*. (2–3). Here, there are six instances of the word *devī* [to be used] in the vocative case for the limbs: *netra-devī* and *astra-devī*.
The Goddess said: Tell me the extraction of the syllables from Prakṛti, as well as the letters and their number, by the knowledge of which the fourteen transformations would be known. (1)
Īśvara said:
Listen, O Goddess, to the great secret which you ask me concerning the letters arising from the mantra of the garland; I shall also state their number. 2.
Having uttered the three *tārās* and the *praṇava*, one should say "Salutation to Tripurasundarī.
After the word "heart" (*hṛdaya*), O Goddess, one should proclaim the word "head" (*śiras*) followed by "Goddess" (*devī*).

There is a *saṃdhi* (euphonic combination) between the two words. This is because [the author] has extracted [the name] from the *Anaṅgakusumā* mantra and so forth by omitting the letter *a*; this serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*). In the same way, the explanations regarding the *saṃdhis* in subsequent passages are to be understood.
Now, he states that the sixteen *Nityās* are to be worshipped within the lines of the triangle and in its center, using three and a quarter verses.
Here, *Vahnivāsinī* is one name. *5*.
Having uttered the word *śikhā* for the goddess of the crest, and from the word *kavaca* for the goddess of the armor;
[then] *netra* for the goddess of the eyes and *astra* for the goddess of the weapon; [then] *kāmeśvarī-bhaga*;
and having uttered the word *mālinī*, one should recite *nityaklinne*.
Bheruṇḍā, Vahnivāsā, Sini, Mahāpadā;
Vajreśvarī, Śivadūtī, Tvaritā, Kulasundarī;
Nityā, Nīlapatākā, Vijayā, and Sarvamaṅgalā. (5–6)

In another tantra, there is also a reading of the word *śiva* as ending in a short vowel (*śivadūta*), yet because the extraction of that very same term is seen in the *Tantrarāja* with a long vowel, the reading here with a long vowel is not untenable. (6) Now, in the space between the central triangle and the eastern triangle, there is the worship of the venerable Guru; and those Gurus are distinguished by the divisions of the *Kālīmata* and the *Kādimata*.

According to each individual school’s tradition, there are three types of descent (*avatāra*) based on the distinctions of *vidyā-avatāra*, *dīkṣā-avatāra*, and [the lineage]. Among these, the gurus for each single descent are individually of three kinds, distinguished by the lineages of the divine (*divya*), the perfected (*siddha*), and the human (*mānava*). Among those, the divine lineages (*divyaugha*) are for the most part entirely real. The perfected lineages (*siddhaugha*) have four divisions each.

The multitudes of human [gurus] are of eight times eight kinds. In some cases, their number may be fewer or greater; however, in the *Kādimata*, they are indeed three by three. Thus, all these multitudes of gurus, according to different traditions, take the form of nine rows and should be worshipped. This has been explained in detail by the venerable Vidyāraṇya-svāmin in the *Vidyārṇava*. In some *tantras*, however, there is only a triad of rows of gurus representing the descent of initiation (*dīkṣāvatāra*).

Then, on the variegated ground of the Great Eternal One garlanded with flames, one should utter the word "Parameśvara" and then proclaim "Parameśvarī. These two are to be worshipped by one who is unable to perform the extensive rite; they are the gurus for the practitioner of the Kāmarāja-vidyā as well as for the practitioner of the Lopāmudrā-vidyā.

The practitioners of the Manu-vidyā and other sciences differ from the practitioners of the Ūrdhvāmnāya, and they also differ among themselves. Since even for each individual there are numerous distinct lineages such as those of Dakṣiṇāmūrti, Ānandabhairava, and others, their gurus are entirely different; thus, no single guru is common to all of them. Therefore, that which pertains to the specific connection with a particular practitioner—(13a)

There are three alternatives: (1) the transcription of that [text] while omitting the *mālā-mantra* for the others; this is like the omission of the mantra "medha" regarding rice when a sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) made of barley is used. Or (2) the recitation of only the other portions by abandoning the word "guru," just as in the ritual of approaching the *aupāsana* fire, the word "gārhapatya" is omitted from the mantra "padaṃ antarikṣam. Or (3) modification (*ūha*) through the substitution of the specific desired term, just as in the case of "juṣṭam agnaye," one says "juṣṭam sūryāya. Thus, whichever of these three positions is appropriate should be adopted according to the rule.

Therefore, for the sake of commonality with all lay practitioners (*upāsaka*), he rescues the previously mentioned number of sages, Vedas, and *āgamas*—namely one hundred and eighty-four—by means of the five verses beginning with "pāda.
Here, even for the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), there is one invocation consisting of two words through the compound *parameśvarī*.
[The others are] *mitrīśamayi*, *ṣaṣṭhīśamayi*, and *uḍḍīśamayi*.

Having uttered "consisting of Caryānātha" and "consisting of Lopāmudrā," [one should say] "consisting of Agastya" at the end of the word; then "consisting of Kālatāpana," having uttered "consisting of Dharmācāra," and "consisting of Muktakeśīśvara. (8–9)
Likewise, O Dīpakalānātha, one should proclaim the word "mayi" (in me);
having uttered "Viṣṇudeva" in relation to me, one should then [proceed] from the word "Prabhākara.
One should say "devaśabdāt mayi" and "tejodevamayī"; at the end of the word "manojadeva," one should say "mayi kalyāṇadevataḥ"; and at "ratnadevamayi," one should say "vāsudevānmayi."

And [there is] the realization of the perfection of *aṇimā*, which consists of the bliss of Śrī Rāma. (12) Then, there is the realization of the perfection of *laghimā*, the perfection of *mahimā*, as well as the perfection of *īśitva* and the realization of the perfection of *vaśitva*. (13)
When *prākāmya-siddhi* has been accomplished, one should recite the word *icchā* after the word *bhukti*.
When *prāpti-siddhi* has been accomplished, one should again recite the word *sarvakāma*.
When *brāhmī* and *māheśvarī* have been stated, one should then proclaim *kaumāri*.

One should then proclaim Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, and Māhendrī. From that point until the end of the section on Agastya, there are seven divine lineages (divyaugha). The four beginning with Kālatāpana constitute the lineage of the Siddhas (siddhaugha). The eight beginning with Viṣṇudeva constitute the lineage of humans (mānavaugha).

The syllable *Śrī* in the *Rāmānanda* [tradition] is merely a component of the mantra; it is not intended solely for the purpose of completing the verse—this is the discernment. Thus, the deities of the limb of dissolution (layāṅga) have been described.

(14a) Now, in the earthen mandala consisting of three lines, named the Wheel that Enchants the Three Worlds (*trailokyamohana-cakra*), there are thirty deities: the ten *siddhis*, the eight Mothers, the ten Mudrās, the one Mistress of the Wheel (*cakranāthā*), and the Yoginī who is their collective form (*samaṣṭirūpa*).
These are described by seven and a quarter verses [verses 9–12].

The awakening to the state of the *aṇimā* perfection is *saṃbuddhi*. And in the phrase "siddha eva ca," the word ending in the vocative (*saṃbudhyaṃta*) is indeed the division [of the compound]. Likewise, in the subsequent instances, the triad of words beginning with *āṇimā* ends in *-mat* and thus takes the feminine suffix *-āp*. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of them ending in a short vowel. Because the word *sarva-* refers here to the word-form itself, it lacks the status of a "name" (*saṃjñā*), and therefore the substitution of *smat* does not occur. 13, 14, 15. Regarding *cāmuṇḍā*: here, the suffix *naṅīp* is not applied after words such as *saṃkṣobhaṇa*, which end in the suffix *lyuṭ*. This is because, in the sense of "she who agitates all," etc., the suffix *yuṅ* is joined when there is a connection to merit (*puṇya*).

Because the suffix *yuc* is prescribed for the agent (*adhikārin*) by the rule [Pāṇini 3.2.150], and because the suffix *ṅīp* would consequently follow from that, the suffix *ṇi* is applied in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlya*), and then *ṅīp* follows from the rules [Pāṇini 4.1.5 and 4.1.7]. Thus, these four names have the vowel *u* as their penultimate sound. Now, with four and a half verses slightly more than that, he extracts the eighteen words consisting of the sixteen deities of the second enclosure situated on the spokes, the sixteen lords of that wheel, and the two *yoginīs*. (16, 17, 18)

The words *ākarṣiṇī* and so forth [in the phrase] "at the sacred site that draws in desire and the rest" all end in the suffix *lyuṭ*; one must not, however, fall into the error of thinking they end in *ṇini*. [This refers to the mantra] *ahaṃkārātmāmṛtaśa...*
"O Cāmuṇḍā, O Mahālakṣmī, O Sarvasaṃkṣobhaṇī;
having uttered [the words] 'Sarvavidrāviṇī' and the word 'Sarvākarṣiṇī';
having uttered 'Sarvavaśaṅkarī' and the word 'Sarvonmādini'. (16)
Having uttered "sarvān mahāṅkuśe" and "sarvakhecari" from all sides,
and having spoken [the mantra] beginning with the word "sarva" into the seed-syllable (bīja),
one should then say "sarvabhikhaṇḍe trailokya" from the Mohanacakra.
One should openly utter the word "Svāminī," and then the term "Yoginī. At the end of the word "Kāmākarṣiṇī," one should proclaim "Buddhyākarṣiṇī.
One should then proclaim "Ahaṃkārākarṣiṇī" and "Śabdākarṣiṇī."
One should recite "attractor of touch" at the end of the word; one should recite "attractor of form. At the end of the word "attractor of taste," one should recite "attractor of smell.
At the end of the word "attractor of mind," one should recite "attractor of fortitude. (20–21)
One should recite the word "memory-attracting" followed by the name;
one should recite the word "seed-attracting" followed by the self.

In the two [verses] following, the instruction for the placement [of the letters] must also be performed, in accordance with the number of syllables that will be described hereafter. Now, he extracts the ten names of the deities of the third enclosure—the eight *cakranāthas* and the two *yoginīs*—in slightly less than three and a quarter verses. (20) (21) (22) (23) (24) (25) Having said "Amṛtākarṣaṇī" (the Attractor of Nectar), and also "Śarīrākarṣaṇī" (the Attractor of the Body).

"O fulfiller of all hopes," "mistress of the circle of rays," (23) "secret yoginī," "from the bodiless one," "with flowers," "girdle of the bodiless," then "intoxication of the bodiless," and "afflicted by the intoxication of the bodiless. (24)
To the north of that, by means of the syllable *naṃga* and the word *rekhā*, one should state the awakening of Naṅgaveginī;
by means of the word *naṃga* and the syllable *aṅkuśa*, one should state the awakening of Mālinī.
And [one should state] the awakening of Sarvasaṃkṣobhaṇācakrasvāminī in a secret manner.
From the word *tara-yoginī* and [the word] *sarva-saṃkṣobhiṇī*;
having uttered *sarva-vidrāviṇī*, [one proceeds] with the word *sarvākarṣiṇī*;
and from the word *sarvāhlādini* and [the word] *sarva-saṃmohinī*. (26–27)
One should recite from sound the word "sarvastambhini," and from sound the word "sarvajṛmbhiṇi"; [one should recite] the word "sarvavaśaṅkari" and from sound the word "sarvarañjani.

Here, by the rule *anaṅ*, the short *a* vowels [of *na*] merge with the preceding long *e* vowels to form the *pūrvarūpa* (single substitute). This is because the term is taught as *naṅ* alone, through the elision of the vowel *a*. Furthermore, by the word *veginīyaśabdāt*, the *yaṇ* substitution is also indicated.
Now, the deities of the fourth enclosure: the Cakranāthas.
After "O you who cause universal intoxication," one should say the word "O you who accomplish all aims.
After the word "O you who possess all prosperity," one should utter the word "O you who fulfill.
Having said "O you who consist of all mantras," [one says] "O you who destroy all dualities."

"Bestower of all good fortune," "Mistress of the wheel of hair," (30) "Yoginī of the tradition," "Bestower of all accomplishments," then "Bestower of all prosperity," and finally, having uttered "She who makes everything dear. (31)
He teaches [the sixteen mudrās] together with the two Yoginīs by means of four verses, each increasing by one quarter-verse at the beginning and end.

Following these are the [mudrās] beginning with Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī. All these words are formed with the suffix *ṇyat* (denoting habit) and end in the feminine suffix *ṅīp*. Consequently, there are ten words whose penultimate vowel is a short *a*.

As for the word *pūraṇī*, the reading with a short *a* as the penultimate vowel is the one most widely accepted; therefore, it should be understood that the form is derived from the root *pṛ* (to fill) with the suffix *lyuṭ* in the sense of the causative (*antarbhāvita-ṇyartha*), and not from the root *pṝ*.
Now, with four verses lacking the first and last quarters [of each], he extracts the twelve names of the Mistress of the Wheel of Deities of the Fifth Enclosure and of the Yoginī:
having stated "Sarvamaṅgalataḥkāriṇī," followed by "sarvācca kāmataḥ," and ending with the words beginning with "prade sarva... and so forth. (16a) [Verses 27–30]
In this context, the words *kāriṇī*, *dāyinī*, and *mocanī* have the vowel *i* as their penultimate sound in their respective positions.
Having spoken *sarvamaṅgalataḥ kāriṇī*, and then *sarvācca kāmataḥ prade*, one should utter the word *duḥkhavimocanī* following the word *sarva*. (32)
One should utter the title "Sarvamṛtyupraśamanī" (the pacifier of all death), "Sarvavighnanivāriṇī" (the warder-off of all obstacles),
"Sarvāṅgasundarī" (she who is beautiful in every limb), "Sarvasaubhāgyadāyinī" (the bestower of all good fortune),
and the title "Sarvārthasādhakacakrasvāminī" (the Mistress of the Wheel that accomplishes all aims). 33.

One should utter: "O Yoginī who has transcended the [lower] bodies," "O Omniscient One" from the word *sarva*, "O Śakti" from the state of universal sovereignty (*sarvaiśvarya*), and "Bestower" (*prade*).
Having spoken thus, one should say: "O Thou consisting of all knowledge, O Destroyer of all diseases. (34–35)

Having described her as being of the nature of the support of all, likewise the remover of all sins, consisting of all bliss, and the embodiment of the protection of all— wherein the letter *A* alone is the pacifier of others, her form being like that of the fulfiller— [the author] now states the twelve names for the first [deity] in the sixth enclosure.
With the first quarter and the three subsequent verses (32,
[the meter is established]. Here, in the words *vināśini* and *svarūpiṇī*, the final vowels of the penultimate syllables remain unchanged.
Now, with two and a quarter verses (35–39), he extracts the ten names of the deities of the seventh enclosure, together with Cakranātha and the Yoginī:

Having uttered [the word] *sarvepsitaprada* ("bestower of all desired objects"), followed by *sarvarakṣākara* ("protector of all") again; then the word *cakrasvāminī* ("mistress of the wheel") at the end, and *nigarbhā* ("from the womb") followed by *yoginī*. (37)
Having uttered the word "Vaśinī," and [the words] "Kāmeśvarī" and "Modinī," then [the words] "Vimalā" and "Cāruṇā," one should speak the word "Jayinī.
Having uttered the word "Sarveśvarī," one should proclaim "Kaulinī. (38)
"O Mistress of the Cakra that removes all diseases"—thus [she is known] in secret.

(39) Now, there are four deities of the weapons; likewise, there are four deities of the eighth enclosure. Including the two, namely the Lord of the Cakra and the Yoginī, he indicates these ten names with two verses accompanied by a quarter-verse each. (40, 41, 42)

Now, with two verses, he sequentially extracts the names of the respective Lords of the Wheels (*cakranātha*) who have been mentioned in the *pratyāvaraṇa* [section]. Here, in the phrase "Tripurāṃ Śrī," there is one long vowel.
[In the phrase] "Siddhibodhanam," it is the vocative case ending in "siddhe.
Because there is no difference between the forms ending in *ikāra* and those ending in *ḍāp* in the vocative case, with the intention of establishing the extraction of the root mantra,
one should first utter "Yoginī," then "Bāṇini" and "Cāpini," then "Pāśinī" and "Aṅkuśinī," and finally "Mahākāmeśvarī. (40)

"O Mahābhagamālinī, [grant] the state of the Great Vajreśvarī, which is the supreme height! O Yoginī, having been addressed as 'Great Śrīsundarī,' you who bestow all accomplishments, [grant] the state of the Mistress of the Wheel from the secret [teaching]! (41)
From "Śrī Śrīpāda," one should utter the word "Mahābhaṭṭārikā.
From "Sarvānandamaya," one should say the word "Cakrasvāminī.
And from "Parāpararahasya," one should pronounce the word "Yoginī. (42–43)
"O Tripurā, O Tripureśī, likewise O Tripurasundarī;
then the word 'Dweller in Tripura' and the word 'Śrī Tripurā';
having uttered 'Mālinī of Tripura,' then [the mantra] that awakens the siddhi of Tripura. (44)
Having uttered the mantra *Tripurā-daṃ*, [one worships] Mahātripurasundarī:
"O Great Queen of the Great Maheśvarīs! O Great, Great One! O Śakti! O Greatly Secret One! And then, O Great, Great One! (45–46).

Even when "siddhe" is stated, [the term] refers specifically to words ending in the suffix *āP*. In that regard, this [interpretation] must be accepted to avoid internal contradiction, because there is a difference in the result regarding those [words] ending in *namaḥ* and so forth. (17b) 45.

Now, he extracts the nine specific epithets of Mahātripurasundarī and the remaining nine syllables of the mantra in three and a half verses. [Verse 46: "In *gupte*, it is the feminine form ending in *ṭāp*; in the vocative, it is not ending in *am*. After *jñatye* and *mahāmahānande*, there follows *mahāmahā*."
In the *spanda*, one should proclaim [the mantra] in the *āśaya* from the great, great sound (*mahāmahāśabda*).
Then, again from the city of the Śrīcakra of the great, great sound, having uttered the word "Samrājñi," one should speak the three-word phrase "namas te. (47–48)
One should also recite the wife of Agni (Svāhā) in reverse order, as well as the three Tārīs.
This Vidyā grants great accomplishment through mere remembrance.
The extraction of the Siddhi-mantra is distinct from the sandhi-conjunction in the Great Word situated at the first syllable of the word *āśaya*; for the word *śaya* itself denotes the hand.
[This is] for the purpose of dispelling the misconception that [the word *samrājñī*] is a constituent part of the mantra.

(47) The word *samrājñī* ends in the feminine suffix *ṅīp*. It is not, however, derived from the word *rāṭ* with the suffix *kvip*. Therefore, the hearing of the final *m*-sound [in *samrājñīm*] is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*). The phrase "three times" refers to the word *padam*;
one must not, however, mistake this for a threefold repetition of the entire phrase "namas te. (48)
In the wife of Agni [the mantra] is *svāhā*, the three *tārās* in reverse order, *ramā*, *māyā*, and *vāgbhava*; the rest is clear.

By this, it is implied that one should recite the mantra preceded by knowledge of its meaning. And it is said in the *Parivasyā-rahasya*: "The mere utterance of a sound devoid of knowledge of its meaning is not fruitful."
Just as fire hidden in ashes blazes forth when the ground is sprinkled [with water], so too does this [mantra] shine.
Now, he praises this knowledge (*vidyā*) with various fruits:
"In the agitation caused by the fear of fire and wind, and during the upheaval of the king and the kingdom, [the practice of] rolling on the ground is indeed directly perceived."
In cases of plunder, fear of thieves, battle, or being swept away by water;
in the mishap of a sea voyage, or fear arising from spirits, ghosts, and the like; and in fear born of epilepsy, old age, disease, death, or rebirth—(50–51).
In fear of ḍākinīs, pūtanās, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and kuṣmāṇḍas;
in the breach of friendship, in fear of planetary influences, in calamity, and in matters of desire;
and in other such misfortunes, a person should remember the garland-mantra (mālāmantra).
Freed from all calamities, one becomes manifestly identical with Śiva.

(53) Regarding the term "all": holding [the breath] in secret is the work of a thief. (50) *Ḍākinī* and others are specific types of *grahas*. *Graha* means fear; specifically, the fear of aquatic *grahas*. (18b)

The calamity of malevolent magic (*abhicārika-vyasana*) is the suffering produced by the rites of killing performed by enemies. (52–53) Adversity (*āpad*) takes the form of imprisonment, seizure, restraint, and so forth.
(54) During a time of adversity, one is unable to perform the daily worship in its full detail.
By a single recitation alone, one obtains the fruit of daily worship.
This garland-mantra, attainable through great fortune, bestows accomplishment instantly;
consisting of thirty-one thousand syllables, it is capable of enchanting the three worlds. (54–55)
Having known this, a person shall attain the fulfillment of all their intentions.

[This is] the mantra of the goddess Lalitā of great splendor, consisting of one thousand three hundred and nine syllables; the analysis of the compound is based on the elision of the middle term (*madhyamapadalopa*). 55–56.

He is the one from whom there is the accomplishment (*siddhi*) of all intentions (*saṃkalpa*), that is, those things which have become objects of one's desires. The distinction is as follows: by the first term "Tripurasundarī," by the sixteenth term "Mahānityā" [referring to the Nityā], by the term "Mahāśrīsundarī," by the three terms beginning with "Śrī-Śrī-Mahābhaṭṭārikā," and by the ten terms beginning with "Mahātripurasundarī"—these sixteen terms taken together—there is the description of Lalitā alone; whereas the description of the deities of the nine enclosures (*navāvaraṇa*) is by others. 56.

He is the domain and object of the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*) of the Vedas and the knowledge section (*jñānakāṇḍa*) of the Vedāntas. (19a) He is the secret form and object of all the scriptures (*āgamas*) belonging to the section on spiritual practice (*upāsanākāṇḍa*). 57–58.
The eight qualities beginning with *aṇimā* constitute sovereignty (*aiśvarya*); by means of that, "delighting" (*rañjana*) consists in the assumption of manifold forms.
From this material nature (*prakṛti*), having awakened to the Power (*śakti*) whose form is the unified enumeration [of all things], one becomes the object of the Vedas and Vedānta.

The meaning of the secrets of all the scriptures, the destroyer of sins through mere remembrance; this most excellent Mālā-vidyā of Lalitā, the Great Goddess, brings men under control, subdues even kings, and effects the enchantment of women. (57–58)
The sovereignty of qualities such as *aṇimā* and others, which is delightful and the destroyer of sin;

likewise, that which arises from the host of deities and mantras of each respective enclosure (*āvaraṇa*), consisting of the garland-mantra (*mālāmantra*), is the secret proclaimed as the supreme abode. (59)
From this, the origin of fourteen other garlands [is derived].
Ending in the accusative, dative, and vocative cases, they consist of three, six, and five [syllables] respectively;
furthermore, five, five, and five [more], consisting of feminine, masculine, and neuter pairs.
The wish-fulfilling trees (kalpataru) consist of the three qualities (triguṇa); they are the eternal collective manifestations of the Goddess.
When recited in sequence according to the Nityā-krama, they bestow the Great Eternal Self (mahānityātman). [62] The mantras... [60]

In the fifteen garlands, for each group of five, there is one [verse] ending in the nominative case, three ending in the accusative, two ending in the dative, and two ending in the vocative; thus, there are six [verses per group]. Since there are six [groups], and each provides the desired object like a wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpadruma*) because it grants its intended meaning, these constitute three sets of five.

In heaven, however, there are only five celestial trees: the Mandāra and Pārijāta, along with the three Kalpa-vṛkṣas. Within these, the fifteen mantras—consisting of the triads from Kāmeśvara to Citrā and forming the collective totality (samaṣṭi) of the fifteen—are to be recited in sequence on their respective lunar days (tithis), beginning with Pratipad and ending with Pūrṇimā; the meaning is that this brings about the attainment of the very nature of the Great Daily Rite (Mahānityā) of Tripurasundarī. Now, he provides an easy-to-understand method for knowing the number of syllables for each of the fourteen Vikṛtis, using eighty-one names ending with "Sāmrājñī" [in two and a half verses].

By "with a hundred nominal stems" (*prātipadika*), it means by that same number. [The formula is: "I worship the sandals of the color of sprouts; *namaḥ*! *svāhā*! I offer libations! Victory, victory!"—thus for the sprouts. One should multiply the syllables of these [names] by the numbers nine, two, and four. Then, to that total of multiplied numbers, one should add the sixteen syllables of the name, the thousand and sixteen syllables of the *Nityās*, and the fifteen [syllables]. [This applies to] the names of the *prakṛti-mantras* and so forth.

(20a) The meaning is that one should combine the six syllables at the end with the nine syllables, thus merging them into the stated aggregate. Although this requirement to join the syllables of the root mantra is established by the singular expression "one should join," nevertheless, in the case of the *mithuna* mantras, the syllables of the name are inserted twice, whereas the fifteen syllables are inserted only once.

The separate mention is for the purpose of indicating a distinction. From the fourth case-ending (*caturthī*) down to the second, there is an increase of syllables in the nature of the base (*prakṛti*) in the case of feminine names, such as *nityaklinnā* and certain words ending in *-ī* (like *ṭāp*), for example: *nityaklinnāyai*, and so forth. These [feminine forms] number exactly thirty-eight. In their masculine counterparts, however, the base consists of thirty-one syllables plus a thousand.

One should multiply the syllables of the names by those of the sprouts and join them therein. Having separated the vowels of the name, the vowels of the Nityās, and the vowels of the case-endings, one should determine the number of syllables of the resulting modification after resolving the sandhis.

In the *mālās*, however, according to the sequence beginning with "to Tripurasundarī," there is an excess of one vowel in the hundred and twenty-six names. (126) And in the second [mantra], such as "to Susundarī" and "Sundaram," because the number of syllables remains the same as the base form (*prakṛti*), the single syllable "Tripurāśriyam" increases; this is the distinction.

Regarding "junctions" (*saṃdhi*): First, concerning the *prakṛti-mantras*, there are twenty names, beginning with the Weapon Goddess (*astradevī*) and others, which are extremely secret *yoginīs*. Among these, for those names that possess initial vowels (such as *i*), there is an instruction for their conjunction with the final vowel of the preceding name. This occurs through either the *pūrvarūpa* sandhi or by the elision of one vowel; since this [elision] exists even in the *prakṛti*, it is a specific modification (*vikṛti*) made according to the author's intent. However, in the case of the first two—*icchāsiddhi* and *aiśvaryasiddhi*—since there is no elision in the *prakṛti*, in the *vikṛtis* they are recited after the *pallava* such as "I worship" (*pūjayāmi*) or "svāhā," resulting in [forms like] *savarga-dīrgha* or *guṇa*.

Since elision (lopa) is inevitable for both, the addition of the aforementioned number of syllables, such as the *piṇḍa* and so forth, must be performed. It is not the case that the meaning [of the name] has been elevated [to a higher status], nor is the plural form "saṃdhīn" incoherent; for in the mantras of the pairs (*mithuna*), this is established by the elision of two syllables each. Alternatively, the term "vocative" (*saṃbuddhi*) may be understood through the omission of the middle syllable, following the method of taking a portion of a name. In the analysis of the compound *saṃbuddhayaś ca saṃdhī ca*, when a single remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) is formed as "masculine and feminine," the word *saṃdhīn* is used. By this, the elision of fifteen syllables occasioned by the masculine vocative is included.

The example is as follows: For a mantra ending in *namaḥ*, with nine syllables in its *pallava* [expansion], when counted by means of one hundred and eighty-one names, the total becomes one thousand six hundred and twenty-nine (*1629*). In that context, the number of the letters of the names is one thousand fifteen and sixteen (*1016*), and [the count] of feminine forms such as *yavantī* and so forth...

By adding the thirty-eight syllables consisting of the letter *ya* joined with the dative case (*caturthīvibhakti*), and by removing the two syllables used for the vocative (*saṃbuddhi*), there are two thousand six hundred and ninety-six syllables. Or, for example, when the four syllables of the "sprout" (*pallava*) of the mantra ending in "Victory! Victory! (*jayajaya*) are multiplied by the number of names, there are seven hundred and twenty-four; by adding the syllables of those names and the constant number [of other elements], there are one thousand seven hundred.

And it becomes fifty-five. In that regard, in the masculine gender, when there is the elision of the fifty vowels—including the words ending in *in* and *an*, such as *Bhagamālinī*—and the two diphthongs (*saṃdhyakṣara*) used in the vocative case, the total is one thousand seven hundred and three. For example, in the *mithuna-mantra* ending with *svāhā*, by multiplying the pair of syllables of the sprout (*pallava*) by the numbers of male and female names, and by joining the name-syllables twice, there are two thousand seven hundred and seventy-one.
The *atyashṭi* meter exceeds [the previous] on all sides; the *śiśu* is smaller on all sides.
O you who possess the splendor of the number two hundred and twenty-six, increase by ninety-six!

In that regard, when there is the conjunction of the thirty-eight feminine dative forms and the one hundred and twenty-six masculine dative forms, and when the two *saṃdhyakṣara* vowels are elided twice [from the former], the total is one hundred and thirty-nine; in this same manner, the number for the others should also be calculated. (64) Now, for the sake of favoring his devotees, he teaches the number for each: "The garland-mantra (*mālāmantra*) ending in *namaḥ*, which has twelve *mithuna*-deities and is composed in the *atyaṣṭi* meter, is in that [garland]."
Five thousand four hundred and sixty-five syllables are observed [in this]. There is no other *mālāmantra* with more syllables than that, nor one with an equal number of syllables.

The syllables of the pure *mālāmantra* dedicated to the deity Śiva are nine hundred and eighty-one. There is no other mantra equal to or fewer than that. By the mention of "two children" (*śiśudvaya*), the grasping of only the initial syllables of the pure words of Śiva, according to the maxim of "part for the whole" (*nāmaikadeśanyāya*), the fitness for being fewer is to be maintained; this is an indication for one who desires another task.

The garland-mantra (mālāmantra) consists of the names of the Śaktis ending in *namaḥ*, and its meter is *uṣṇik*. In this regard, there is no dispute concerning the dative singular forms of words ending in *ṭāp* or *ṅīp*.
Furthermore, for the words *siddhi*, *yoni*, *śakti*, and *jñapti*, which end in *ṅīp*, their forms are likewise feminine; they do not take masculine forms such as *siddhayaḥ* and so forth.
Consequently, there are two thousand six hundred and ninety-six syllables (*akṣara*). 65.

(22a) "Thirty" is used in the instrumental case in the sense of accompaniment (*sahārthe*); there are fourteen [syllables] that break the *gotra*. In the *anuṣṭubh* [meter], the *svāhānta-śaktimālā* [consists of] one thousand forty-one and twenty-nine [syllables]. This means there are 1,429 syllables. The fourth [line] is joined with the word "namas. These are the words mentioned immediately below.

The *uṣṇih* and *anuṣṭubh* [meters]. If the numerical values of these two are added together, they constitute respectively the number of syllables in the *sarasvatī-devatyamālā* and the *vivasvādityarṣikamālā*: namely, two thousand seven hundred and eighty-four (2,784). The syllables of the *namaḥ-anta śivamālā* are one thousand five hundred and seventeen (1,517); the syllables of the *svāhā-anta śivamālā* are as follows: [1,517]. Of these two—

Regarding words ending in *da*, *ta*, *ṭā*, *va*, *taṅ*, and *ī*: for those words ending in a short *ā*, their own form [is used], as in *bheruṇḍāya* and *sundarāya*. But for feminine nouns ending in *ī*, such as *bhagamālinī*, [the form is *bhagamāline*]. For those ending in *i*, such as *siddhi*, [the form is *siddhaye*]. As in *mahālakṣmyai* and *vātapramyai*, [the forms become] *mahālakṣme* and *tripure śriyaḥ śriye*. For the word *saṃrājñī*, [the form is] *saṃrājāya* and not *saṃrājñe*, because in the present context there is no occurrence of the root *rāj* with the suffix *kvip*.

The letter *m* [is substituted] for the final syllable of *samaḥ* when followed by *rājani*. Here, as in the original Vedic text (*prakṛti*), this is purely an archaic usage (*chāndasa*). It should be understood that even though it ends in a consonant here, its status as a modification of a word ending in a vowel (*anta-śabda-vikāra*) is not lost. 66.

The oceans are four; the arrows are five; the horses are seven; the moon is one. The arrangement of numbers proceeds from right to left, and there is an increment [of place value]. Thus, it is one thousand seven hundred fifty-four (1754). There are syllables for each of the two mantras: the *tarpaṇānta-śakti* and the *śiva-mālā*. Regarding these two, the sage of the first is Āditya; the designation of the two ends is made by the words "Āditya" and "Pūṣāditya. Herein lies the *prakṛti*.
These two, Sarasvatī and Vivasvant, [are described] by twenty-nine Anuṣṭubh verses;
these two exceed [the previous total] by eighty-eight.
Aṛyaman and Pūṣan [are described] by verses numbering four hundred and sixty-four.

When the ear and speech faculties are diminished by the mother-letters (*mātṛkā*) and the moon (*indu*) respectively, there are seven hundred and twenty-four syllables of the *pallava* type. By employing the form ending in the accusative case as "Tripurāśriyam," and combining this one [syllable], there are seventeen hundred and fifty-six. When joined with that through euphonic combination (*saṃdhi*), two syllables beginning with "Siddhi" are subtracted for the sake of the state of being the Lord (*īśitva*).

This is the distinction. In this very same number, when diminished by fifty-one through the *mātṛkā*, it becomes the number of syllables contained in the *śivamantra* located at the end of the *ṛṣika* [and] the presiding deity of the sense organ of hearing (*śrotrindriya*). However, when diminished by exactly one moon (*indu*), it becomes the number of syllables in the *śaktimantra* located at the end of the *ṛṣika* [and] the presiding deity of the faculty of speech (*vāgindriya*).

The number of syllables in the mantra is as follows: the *jayānta-śiva-mantra* consists of one thousand seven hundred and three syllables (1,703). The second mantra likewise consists of one thousand seven hundred and fifty-three syllables (1,753); this is the distinction. Here, the increase in the number of *pallava*-syllables added according to the original form is exactly the same in both cases, because there is no difference in the fact that the two *jaya*s and the word *tarpayāmi* each consist of four syllables.

The word *śriyam* ending in the accusative case is employed as a single syllable in one instance, whereas in the other, together with that same syllable, fifteen syllables are brought forward by virtue of being used in the masculine vocative; such is the justification. Halika is Śiva, possessing [the number] one thousand less nineteen.

That same [mantra] doubled is the thirty-five-syllable *Hṛdayeśvara*. It has Śiva, known as Halika, as its presiding deity; it is the *Śuddhaśivamālā* mantra. Due to its feminine grammatical gender (*strīliṅga*), it lacks five syllables when compared to the vocative form in the masculine gender (*pulliṅga*).

*Kāśī* consists of one hundred and nine syllables. (981) The *mithunamālā-mantra*, which has Śiva as its heart-deity and lord, possesses twice the number of syllables because it is a composite form of male and female; thus, it becomes [one hundred and nine] plus thirty-five [making one hundred and forty-four]. Regarding its derivation: *prakṛti* is the form of the mantra of pure Śakti. (1031) The mantra of pure Śiva is [one hundred and nine]. (981) Their conjunction is [two hundred and eighteen]. (2012) Here, since the fifteen syllables of the *saṃpuṭa* are to be added only once, there is a deficiency in that portion due to the doubling [of the other part]; therefore, one [syllable] is [added].
One thousand nine hundred and ninety-seven (1,997) [syllables] arise.

(68) That very mantra of Śuddhaśiva is precisely the number of its syllables; that is to say, it amounts to that. The suns are twelve (12). There are two thousand nine hundred and thirty-one (2,931) syllables. This means they belong to the mantra ending in *svāhā* which consists of a pair [of mantras] dedicated to the deity Śiva known as Karuṇākara. The proof for this has already been cited previously. Sarasvatī.

The number of syllables in the mantras ending in *namaḥ* in the masculine gender was stated previously. Doubling that number and then subtracting one hundred and three results in five thousand four hundred and sixty-five (5,465). These constitute all the syllables of the garland-mantra (*mālāmantra*) ending in *mithuna-namaḥ*.

When the *namaḥ* at the end of *Śakti* and the *namaḥ* at the end of *Śiva* are joined, fifteen syllables are formed in a "casket" (*saṃpuṭa*) arrangement; by removing them once, those same [syllables] are established. (69) This amounts to two and a half [thousand]. [That is to say: horses minus seven—that is, three thousand four hundred and ninety-three (3,493)—is the meaning. The "Lord of Beauty" (*Lāvaṇyanāyaka*) is the mantra of the couple ending with the libation (*tarpaṇa*). Its derivation is established through the doubling of the libations immediately following Śiva and Śakti, resulting in fifteen [libations].

That very number mentioned in the first half [of the verse] is thus the count for the Jayānta-mithuna-mālā: three thousand four hundred and forty-one syllables (3441). When the union of Śiva and Śakti is tripled, it is five; yet when diminished by the sun (twelve), that very one is the Compassionate One (Karuṇākara).
The two Sarasvatīs are less than one hundred, yet they are more than everything else for us. (69) These numbers of syllables in the garlands have been declared by me individually;
taken together, they are equal to the number of the Nidhis, the Aśvins, the Vedas, and the fires. (70)
And when ten are subtracted, that [number] is established.

Having combined the individual counts of fifteen garlands, having formed a collection and unified them into a single heap—this is the remainder of the sense. The treasures are nine; the Dasras are two; the horses are seven; the Vedas are four; the fires are three. [The total is] thirty-four thousand.
(24b) Seven hundred and twenty-nine is the total sum of all the garlands. This is the number of syllables.

This count is intended for the perpetual recitation (*nityajapa*); however, regarding specific optional recitations (*kāmyajapa*), we shall explain it as being in the form of the arrows, serpents, horses, Vedas, and fires [i.e., 5-8-7-4-3]. (71)
This aggregate of phonemes, the total sum of all that has arisen, has just now been declared. This aggregate of phonemes is the manifest Mātṛkā;
by knowing this aggregate of phonemes, one becomes the aggregate of phonemes oneself.
Through the thorough knowledge of each of those respective numbers, that eternal [Mātṛkā] becomes pleased. (71)

Form itself is the practitioner. This knowledge of the number [of these] brings about identity with Śabdabrahman; the sense is that as long as Brahman extends, so far does the Goddess of Speech (Vāgīśvarī) extend, because for her too there is great fruit. Since these garlands have arisen sequentially from the fifteen phonemes of the Kādividyā, he says "tattat" (each respective), meaning that through the knowledge of their number, one attains the grace of each respective Nityā among those beginning with Kāmeśvarī and ending with Citrā, who preside over those respective phonemes. 72.

Then, preceded by knowledge, having understood the application (*viniyoga*) of the ṛṣis, meters, deities, and functions for all [the mantras] therein— encompassing the collection of fifteen garlands consisting of three pentads through the division of the Śakti-Śiva couple, as well as the mantra of the first garland by means of the elision of the prefix *ā*— he makes his own nature ever-new and eternally fresh.
"Aho! Even that which has been praised many times becomes ever-new when it is made an object of affection; thus say the learned. (72) This means:

making [the Goddess] the object of devotion (*bhakti*) consisting of very firm attachment preceded by the knowledge of Her majesty. Being one of firm devotion, whoever—whether a member of the *brāhmaṇa* and other castes, or another such as a *śūdra*, or even one of mixed caste—is constantly intent upon the worship of the *pañcadaśamālā*, he attains the supreme form of the Goddess, which those who know the Supreme Brahman recognize. This is the meaning.

Alternatively, it is stated in the *Rudrayāmala*, in the chapter on secrets (*rahasyādhyāya*), that the fact that each syllable of the *Śrīvidyā* and other mantras takes the form of the number nine is to be understood from the mouth of one's own guru. Similarly, here the meaning is that one should worship after learning from the mouth of the teacher that the written syllables possess a correspondence with the number nine. [Then follows: "The aggregate of fifty-one garlands of five-triplets, preceded by the knowledge of the beginning and the end..."

One should understand that among the *mātṛkās*, one should know the ninefold nature (*navātmatā*) in all the letters except for the fourth letter of the *ca*-group and the *ṭa*-group, and the second letter of the *pa*-group— just as one who is devoted to constant worship transforms oneself into a new form.
When the beginning and the end are considered, it is because those very same syllables are present therein. This is what he says with the words "beginning and end.

Alternatively, in all cases, a recitation (*japa*) consisting of a number such as one hundred or one thousand is prescribed; since all of that constitutes a single collective whole, when the state of being "eight more than [that]" is prescribed, it is clearly for the sake of its nine-fold nature, as is evident in the authoritative texts (*ākara*). Thus, here too, the meaning is that after having recited even fifteen [times] on the rosary (*mālā*), one should subsequently recite the fifteenth [mantra] eight times. [This is stated] in the *Mālinīvijayatantra* and other works.

It has been established [in the *Setubandha* and other works] by us that mantras are devoid of beginning and end, as expressed in the passage beginning with "like an autumnal cloud," because their secret nature consists in being without beginning or end. Regarding the term "beginning and end": for instance, it is universally accepted everywhere that "nine-fold selfhood" (*navātmatva*) means precisely having nine components.
