This is because such nine-fold selfhood is taught in various places regarding the wheel, the yoginis, the preliminary rite (*puraścaryā*), the Goddess, and the body of the worshipper. Therefore, here too, in the enumeration of the syllables of the collection of mantras—

Alternatively, having produced [the number] by increasing it in its own place according to the logic of the "staff-measured" (*daṇḍakalita*) sequence consisting of nine parts, that would result in thirty-four thousand seven hundred and twenty-nine;
this would occur by dividing that total number by nine. However, that is not possible here. Dividing by nine yields three thousand eight...

Even with five hundred and eighty, there remains only seven; for it is impossible to divide that [number] by nine with a remainder. Even if one divides the one hundred and twenty syllables of the fifteen-verse hymn being recited by groups of seven for the sake of reaching the number "eight plus one" (one hundred and eight), a remainder of one syllable is inevitable. Therefore, that state of being "eight plus one" must be accomplished through the recitation of the sixteen-verse hymn (*ṣoḍaśī*) alone; for only in that case is the symmetry of the number maintained. Consequently, [the total] consists of three thousand, eight hundred, and seventy-three syllables.
Each one— a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, a Śūdra, or even anyone else—
attains the supreme form of Mahātripurasundarī. (73)

Thus, through the expansion of the ninefold nature (*navātmatā*) in its own place, [the mantra] comes to be. According to the logic of the "repeated stick" (*daṇḍakalita-nyāya*), each individual portion consisting of nine syllables becomes of that same number; thus, in both cases, the ninefold nature remains as the remainder. Regarding the phrase "at the beginning and end," it is just as before. Alternatively, the knowledge of the sixteen-syllable [mantra] which is to be recited once at the beginning and at the end, as well as the knowledge of the number of its syllables mixed with the number of the beads on the rosary, must be described based on the meaning of *om*, since it cannot otherwise be logically accounted for.

Since there is no other scriptural authority (*kalpaka*) for the injunction of "eight plus one" (*aṣṭottara*) as a way to establish the state of being ninefold (*navātmakatā*), and since the *ṣoḍaśī* consists of twenty-six syllables,

it is possible to establish the state of being ninefold by taking the aforementioned number— obtained by adding the doubled count of that [twenty-six] to the seven [syllables of the *saptākṣarī*]— and then allowing for a deficiency of eight.

Thus, there are five explanations. However, we state the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). It is beyond dispute that when the previously mentioned total number—measured by the treasure, the weapon, the horse, and the fire—is combined, it becomes ninefold through the addition of fifty-six. And such a [number] as sixteen should not be employed to be increased by doubling; for there is a clear statement to that effect. Rather, one sees exactly that many optional syllables among the *mātrās* alone. For instance, the words for accomplishment (*siddhipadāni*)...

There are ten *śakti* words, two *yoni* words, and one each for the *jñapti* word; thus, for the fourteen words, forms ending in the feminine dative case—such as *siddhyai* and so forth—are used. These are either two-syllable forms like *siddhyai* and so on, or three-syllable forms like *siddhaye* and so on, according to option (*vikalpa*). However, in the previous calculation of syllables, only the two-syllable forms were taken for those respective mantras. In the alternative of using the three-syllable forms, the syllables increase to fourteen. Regarding those [mantras] ending in *svāhā* or *namaḥ*, the case-ending is according to tradition (*sāṃpradāyikī*).

Because there is no distinction between the two sides of the injunction: in these four mantras—namely, those ending in *śakti* and *namaḥ*, and those ending in *svāhā* and *mithuna namaḥ*—there is an increase of fourteen [mantras] for each individually by way of option, resulting in a total of fifty-six.

This [practice] occurs by combining the first pentad and the third pentad, but not in the middle pentad; for there, due to the absence of terms such as *strīliṅga* and *siddhi*, conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is impossible. To indicate this, it is stated that [the practice] is "preceded by knowledge of the beginning and the end. Furthermore, the natural implication of designating [the practice] as three pentads, rather than stating "of the fifteen," is also consistent only with this position.

Likewise, the phrase "intent upon the constant worship" (*nityopāstiparaḥ*) is intended to enjoin another form of meditation based on the nature of the fifteen *Nityās*, and is not a mere restatement (*anuvāda*) of what has already been taught. Now, as for the word "atha" (now/then), it [indicates] the state of being ninefold...

"Intent on the conceptual meditation (*bhāvanā*) on the nature of the fifteen. Or rather, this is the meaning: "When she [the demoness] has been slain, when that wicked one is killed, and when the lion has been struck down, come quickly, having bound and seized that Mother (*Ambikā*)," as seen in the commentary on a verse from the *Devīmāhātmya*. Likewise, according to the subsequent enumeration, there are two thousand three hundred and nineteen syllables (*2319*) even with a division into fifteen parts, just as there are with nine. Each part thus consists of this number of syllables. Therefore, if one is intent on either of these meditations, it is said in the *Uktamālācatuṣṭaya*:

One should recite "siddhaye" [for the sake of accomplishment]. As for others, however, the rule that they should recite "sidhyai" and so forth is established; thus everything is consistent. (73) [End of section] The Lord of Syllables. The number of syllables is preceded by knowledge. Worship is the adoration of Tripurasundarī.

This is the procedure for the recitation of the *mālā-mantra*, preceded by the conclusion. By the word "necessarily," the previous verse indicates that there is a transgression (*pratyavāya*) for the practitioner if this is not performed. Even though [these mantras] are not to be revealed, even to a qualified person; he who studies these syllables has studied the entirety of the Veda.
If a practitioner of Śrīvidyā does not know these mantra-garlands— the Smṛtis, the Purāṇas, and all the Tantras as well—
then their practice yields no fruit; it is like offering many oblations into ashes.
Therefore, these fifteen garlands must certainly be known;
though they are not to be disclosed, they have been spoken by me solely out of affection for you, O Śivā.
Thus ends the second chapter in the *Śrī Lalitāpariśiṣṭatantroddhāra*.

"To one devoid of devotion. "Only through love for you. By the phrase "having known his devotion fixed upon that," it is indicated that the author himself possesses the qualification to teach, as he is a devotee of the Mālā-mantra even while being a worshipper of Śiva. By this, it is also implied as an instruction that another teacher, too, should examine the devotion of a seeker before imparting [the mantra] to that seeker. May all be auspicious!

Thus ends the final chapter, the extraction of the numerical value of the script (*lipi-saṃkhyoddhāra*), in this commentary on the *Gurukalā*, composed by Bhāskara— the son of Śrī Gaṃbhīrādhvarin— who is proficient in the method for extracting the key (*kīla*) from the basket of the jewel-strings (*mālāmaṇipiṭaka*). 1.
Thus ends the second chapter in the commentary on the extraction of the Mālā-mantra from the *Śrī-lalitā-pariśiṣṭa-tantra*.
